fr.elements: Main Building; Front Driveway; Vehicle Parking Area; Open Green Space; Landscaped Area; Dense Vegetation; Perimeter Fencing; Access Road; Detached Structure; Open Terrain
fr.considerations: Single Access Point; Long Driveway; Dense Vegetation; Limited Rear Access; Open Terrain
fr.recommendations: Ensuring the single access point and extended driveway remain unobstructed could significantly improve apparatus entry and egress during emergency operations. Maintaining adequate driveway width and vertical clearance along the full length of the approach would support larger emergency vehicles accessing both the main building and detached structure. Clearly marking the access point with visible address signage may assist responding units in locating the property quickly, particularly given the length of the driveway. Where perimeter fencing restricts movement around the rear of the structures, identifying or designating an alternative secondary access route could enhance responder maneuverability and support staging operations on the open terrain areas of the property.

wildfire.conditions: Structure Surrounded by Vegetation; Scattered Shrubs; Scattered Shrubs; Scattered Trees; Scattered Trees; Long Driveway; Single Access Route; Brush Adjacent to Structure; Mixed Vegetation Cover; Fuel Continuity; Open Terrain; Brushland Interface
wildfire.recommendations: Reducing the concentration of brush and shrubs immediately adjacent to the structure would improve defensible space and may reduce the opportunity for fire to spread directly to the building. Creating and maintaining separation between scattered shrubs, trees, and the structure perimeter could further reduce fuel continuity across the property. Along the driveway, managing vegetation on both sides to maintain adequate width and vertical clearance would support firefighter access and improve conditions for emergency vehicle movement along the single access route. Given the mixed vegetation cover and brushland interface conditions surrounding the property, maintaining an open buffer zone around improvements where feasible could reduce structure exposure and support suppression operations. Periodic vegetation management within the immediate structure zone, with attention to shrubs making contact with or growing close to walls, eaves, and other structural components, would contribute to long-term wildfire resilience.
